introduction-beyond-basic-matching.core: Production regex has to handle context-dependent matches (lookarounds), stay fast on hostile input (atomic groups, possessive quantifiers) and stay maintainable (named groups, non-capturing groups).

first_principles.problem: Simple patterns match too much or too little on messy logs, and one bad pattern can freeze a service (ReDoS).
truths: Backtracking engines can take exponential time.
Regexes are read far more than they're written.

analogy.title: A precise search tool vs. Find/Replace
analogy.story: Find/Replace finds the text; a precision tool finds it only in the right context, quickly and safely.
analogy.breaks: Some problems (nested structures like HTML) still need a real parser.

example.title: Parsing a messy log
example.outcome: regex that works on real data.

check.a: Regular-expression denial of service: inputs that trigger catastrophic backtracking and consume CPU.

lookaheads-peeking-into-the-future.core: A lookahead checks what follows the current position without consuming it: `(?=...)` requires it and `(?!...)` forbids it. It's ideal for 'match X only if followed by Y' and for password rules.

first_principles.problem: You want 'timeout' only when followed by 'error', without including 'error' in the match.
truths: Some conditions depend on what comes next.
Several lookaheads can test independent conditions.
derivation: Stack them at the start for **AND conditions**.

analogy.title: Peeking at the next word before highlighting
analogy.story: You read ahead to check, then highlight only the current word.
analogy.breaks: Overusing lookaheads makes patterns hard to read. Sometimes two passes are clearer.

example.title: Password policy in one regex
example.scenario: At least one digit and one uppercase, 12+ characters.

check.a: 'foo' when it is not immediately followed by 'bar'.

lookbehinds-checking-the-past.core: A lookbehind checks what precedes the current position: `(?<=...)` requires and `(?<!...)` forbids. It's perfect for extracting values after a label, like the number after 'latency='.

first_principles.problem: You want the number after 'latency=' without capturing the label, and you need to avoid matching '$' amounts in one specific context.
derivation: Check the **engine**: Python's re requires fixed-width lookbehind.

analogy.title: Glancing back at the sign before reading the price
analogy.story: You confirm the sign says 'Price:' and then read only the number.
analogy.breaks: Variable-length lookbehinds aren't supported in many engines (Python re, older JS).

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No post-processing to strip the label.

check.q: Why might `(?<=a+)b` fail in Python's re?
check.a: Python's re only supports fixed-width lookbehind patterns.

atomic-grouping-stopping-catastrophic-ba.core: Nested quantifiers like `(a+)+` can make backtracking engines try exponentially many paths on near-miss input. Atomic groups `(?>...)` and possessive quantifiers `a++` refuse to backtrack into what they matched.

first_principles.problem: A validation regex on user input hangs the CPU at 100% on a 30-character string, which is a ReDoS outage.
truths: Backtracking engines retry alternatives on failure.
Ambiguous nested quantifiers multiply the alternatives.
Committing to a match removes the retries.
derivation: Or use a **linear-time engine** (RE2, Rust regex).

analogy.title: A maze runner who never revisits a corridor
analogy.story: A naive runner retries every combination of turns; the atomic runner commits to each corridor and fails fast.
analogy.breaks: Atomic groups change what can match, so they're only safe when backtracking wasn't needed for correctness.

steps.label: Policy
steps.detail: Run untrusted patterns or input through RE2.

code.text:
Bad:   ^(\w+\s?)+$     on 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!'  → seconds/minutes
Good:  ^(?>\w+\s?)+$   → fails instantly

check.q: Why do nested quantifiers cause catastrophic backtracking?
check.a: On failure, the engine tries exponentially many ways to split the input between the inner and outer quantifiers.

named-capture-groups-making-matches-read.core: Named groups `(?P<name>...)` (Python) or `(?<name>...)` label each capture, so code reads `m['status']` instead of `m.group(4)`, and adding a group doesn't shift every index.

first_principles.problem: Six months later nobody knows what group(3) means, and inserting a new group breaks every index.

analogy.title: Labelled jars vs. numbered jars
analogy.story: 'Jar 3' tells you nothing; 'Sugar' tells you everything, even after you rearrange the shelf.
analogy.breaks: Syntax differs between engines (Python's ?P<> vs PCRE/JS ?<>).

example.title: Parsing an access log line

code.text:
LOG = re.compile(r"""
  (?P<ip>\S+)\s.*?\s
  "(?P<method>[A-Z]+)\s(?P<path>\S+)[^"]*"\s
  (?P<status>\d{3})
""", re.X)
m = LOG.search(line); print(m["path"], m["status"])

example.outcome: regex that stays readable for years.

check.q: Why are named groups more robust than numbered ones?
check.a: Adding or reordering groups doesn't change the names your code uses.

non-capturing-groups-grouping-without-th.core: Use `(?:...)` when you need parentheses only for grouping (alternation, quantifiers). It avoids capture overhead and keeps group numbering focused on the data you want.

first_principles.problem: `(http|https)://(www\.)?(\S+)` puts the domain in group 3, plus two captures nobody uses.
truths: Captures cost memory and shift indexes.
Grouping and capturing are separate needs.
derivation: Combine with **named groups** for the important parts.

analogy.title: Brackets in maths vs. labelled answers
analogy.story: Brackets organise the calculation; you only write down the answers you need.
analogy.breaks: The performance gain is usually small. The main win is clarity.

code.text:
Before: (http|https)://(www\.)?([^/]+)      → host in group 3
After:  (?:https?)://(?:www\.)?(?P<host>[^/]+) → m['host']

check.a: When you need grouping for alternation or quantifiers but don't need the matched text.
